title: US charitable funds are a time machine: claim the tax break now, decide the donations later
dek: It's a legal 'charity time machine': put money in and get an immediate tax deduction, while deciding whom to donate to and when to do so years later—Anthropic employees' future massive donations will likely flow through this system.
why: For anyone wanting to understand how American charitable giving actually works: how DAFs decouple tax deductions from donations in time, and why writing checks is paradoxically the optimal approach.
who: Entrepreneurs and charity professionals interested in US tax law and philanthropic infrastructure, plus anyone curious how AI wealth will flow into the charitable sector.

points.h: Tax exemption is the foundation of the charitable subsidy
points.body: US nonprofits have the same legal structure as ordinary companies—they can rent offices, hire employees, open bank accounts, and be sued. The only real distinction is tax treatment: donors can deduct contributions against income, and nonprofits themselves pay no income tax and are exempt from sales tax in many states. These two linked privileges created an entire infrastructure unique to nonprofits. The donor-advised funds and specialized accounting systems discussed below all stem from this arrangement.

points.h: A receipt takes two minutes; the industry burns billions
points.body: The IRS requires written confirmation from a nonprofit for donations over $250, but this receipt is simple enough for a seven-year-old to produce in a minute or two. Yet the reality is that nonprofit record-keeping and supporting software burn billions of dollars in professional labor annually. Another hidden requirement: nonprofits must file Schedule B at year-end, disclosing all donors whose annual gifts exceed $5,000 (with names anonymized). This guards against both receipt fraud and wealthy donors using nonprofits as vehicles to redirect their own wealth.

points.h: Donor-advised funds are literally a time machine
points.body: For someone with a sudden windfall—say, from selling a company—the timing is awkward: the income arrives, taxes are due, but the desire to donate comes years later, yet income tax is calculated annually. Donor-advised funds (DAF) solve this mismatch: money deposited is immediately counted as a donation and generates a tax deduction in that year, but the choice of recipient and timing can be deferred—you simply 'advise' later. Legally, it's an independent nonprofit, but to the donor it functions like a financial institution that can bend time. Fidelity Charitable alone has nearly 400,000 donors and has distributed nearly $120 billion to other nonprofits.

points.h: A DAF can legally ignore your donation 'advice'
points.body: Once money enters a DAF account, it legally belongs to the DAF, which can deploy it according to its own charitable mandate. Donors think they are 'recommending' that the DAF fund a particular organization, but in theory the DAF could ignore this entirely. In practice, nearly all DAFs faithfully follow donor recommendations—this trust is what allows DAFs to function. This is not a regulatory loophole but rather a deliberately designed system built to honor public intent.

points.h: DAFs send checks to nonprofits—which is actually optimal
points.body: Even though DAF accounts can execute wires and ACH transfers, a substantial share of distributions still go out via paper check. The reason: writing a check requires only the recipient's official name and the ability to put the check in their hands; you assume they'll deposit it quickly. No advance coordination needed, no recipient consent required. Nonprofit names, addresses, and tax-exempt status are all public IRS records, so a DAF can mail a check directly using this information—no need for the nonprofit to answer a call or reply to an email first.

points.h: Nonprofit software foreshadows a broader structural shift
points.body: Beyond DAFs on the donor side, nonprofits themselves rely on specialized accounting software to handle regulatory requirements that are inherently simple yet have been turned into a complex business. This is not unique to nonprofits: in any field with a few high-frequency, tightly regulated requirements, software systems will increasingly handle compliance instead of relying on professional expertise alone. Capital will follow software, not the other way around.

points.h: Anthropic made its 3x employee match unlimited
points.body: Most companies cap their matching donations at a few thousand dollars per year. Anthropic made a costly choice: 3x matching with no practical cap. The stated intention was to let ordinary employees give away as much as founders with special equity structures could. This means Anthropic employees could collectively donate on the order of hundreds of billions, with the company matching at 3x—a commitment no one anticipated when making this pledge how expensive it would become.
